Gorenstein algebras and toric bundles

Askold Khovanskii    Leonid Monin
Abstract

We study commutative algebras with Gorenstein duality, i.e. algebras AA equipped with a non-degenerate bilinear pairing such that ⟨a​c,b⟩=⟨a,b​c⟩\langle ac,b\rangle=\langle a,bc\rangle for any a,b,c∈Aa,b,c\in A. If an algebra AA is Artinian, such pairing exists if and only if AA is Gorenstein. We give a description of algebras with Gorenstein duality as a quotients of the ring of differential operators by the annihilator of an explicit polynomial (or more generally formal polynomial series). This provides a calculation of Macaulay’s inverse systems for (not necessarily Artinian) algebras with Gorenstein duality. Our description generalizes previously know description of graded algebras with Gorenstein duality generated in degree 1.

Our main motivation comes from the study of even degree cohomology rings. In particular, we apply our main result to compute the ring of cohomology classes of even degree of toric bundles and the ring of conditions of horospherical homogeneous spaces.

1 Introduction

In this paper we study Macaulay’s inverse systems of algebras with Gorenstein duality. We say that an algebra AA over a field 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} has a Gorenstein duality if there exists a non-degenerate bilinear pairing on AA such that ⟨a​c,b⟩=⟨a,b​c⟩\langle ac,b\rangle=\langle a,bc\rangle for any a,b,c∈Aa,b,c\in A. If algebra AA is a finite dimensional vector space over 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}, such a pairing exists if and only if AA is a Gorenstein ring.

Let 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} be a field of characteristic 00 and consider a polynomial ring R=𝐤⁡[x1,…,xn]R={\mathbf{k}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Recall that the polynomial differential operator with constant coefficients is a differential operator on RR of the form

D=∑i1,…​inai1​…​ain​(∂/∂x1)i1​…​(∂/∂xn)in.D=\sum_{i_{1},\ldots i_{n}}a_{i_{1}}\ldots a_{i_{n}}\left(\partial/\partial x_{1}\right)^{i_{1}}\ldots\left(\partial/\partial x_{n}\right)^{i_{n}}.

The ring of differential operators with constant coefficients forms a polynomial ring 𝐤⁡[∂/∂x1,…,∂/∂xn]{\mathbf{k}}[\partial/\partial x_{1},\ldots,\partial/\partial x_{n}] which acts naturally on RR.

For an ideal I⊂𝐤⁡[∂/∂x1,…,∂/∂xn]I\subset{\mathbf{k}}[\partial/\partial x_{1},\ldots,\partial/\partial x_{n}] its inverse system is an ideal I⟂⊂RI^{\perp}\subset R of polynomials which annihilate II:

I⟂={f∣D⋅f=0,∀D∈I}⊂R.I^{\perp}=\big\{f\,\mid\,D\cdot f=0,\forall D\in I\big\}\subset R.

Inverse systems were introduced by Macaulay (see [Mac16, Mac27, Grö10]) and is a convenient tool both in commutative algebra and analysis (see [ER12, ER17, ST19, CRS21, MHS21] for some recent developments). In particular, the quotient algebra 𝐤⁡[x1,…,xn]/I{\mathbf{k}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/I is a zero-dimensional Gorenstein ring if and only if I⟂I^{\perp} is a principle ideal [Eis95, Exercise 21.7].

For a finite dimensional vector space VV over 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}, one can identify the ring of differential operators with constant coefficients on VV with symmetric algebra Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V). For a polynomial function f:V→𝐤f:V\to{\mathbf{k}}, let us denote by Ann⁡(f):=⟨f⟩⟂{\mathrm{Ann}}(f):=\langle f\rangle^{\perp} its annihilator in the ring of differential operators with constant coefficients. Thus for any polynomial ff on VV, the factor algebra Sym⁡(V)/Ann⁡(f){\mathrm{Sym}}(V)/{\mathrm{Ann}}(f) has a Gorenstein duality, and every zero-dimensional Gorenstein factor algebra of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) is constructed in this way.

In this paper we extend these results in the following way. First, we extend the above correspondence to non-Artinian commutative algebras with Gorenstein duality over a field of characteristic 00. We show that for a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space VV the factor algebras of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) with Gorenstein duality are in bijection with formal polynomial series on VV (Corollary 3.16). We also give an explicit formula for the generator of the Macaulay’s inverse system of factor algebras of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) with Gorenstein duality (Theorem 4.2).

Our main motivation to study algebras with Gorenstein duality comes from computation of cohomology rings. Indeed, let MM be a smooth closed orientable manifold of even dimension and let

A∗​(M):=⨁i=0(dimℝM)/2H2​i​(M,ℝ),A^{*}(M):=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{(\dim_{\mathbb{R}}M)/2}H^{2i}(M,{\mathbb{R}}),

be the ring of cohomology classes of even degree. Then A∗​(M)A^{*}(M) is a commutative ring with Gorenstein duality given by Poincaré duality on H∗​(M)H^{*}(M). Thus our description of algebras with Gorenstein duality provides a way to compute A∗​(M)A^{*}(M).

Such approach was used to compute the cohomology ring of smooth projective toric varieties in [PK92b] and the cohomology rings of full flag varieties in [Kav11]. These works, however, crucially use that the above cohomology rings are generated in degree 2. Our explicit calculation of Macaulay’s inverse systems of algebras with Gorenstein duality (Theorem 4.2) is applicable for computation of much wider class of cohomology rings. As an illustration, we apply Theorem 4.2 to computation of the rings of cohomology classes of even degrees of toric bundles (Theorem 5.8). In particular, this includes the computation of cohomology rings of smooth, toroidal horospherical varieties and the ring of conditions of horospherical homogeneous spaces (Theorem 5.9).

1.1 Organization of the paper

Section 2 provides the necessary background on algebras with Gorenstein duality. In Section 3 we define spaces of polynomials and formal polynomial series on (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space VV and study the action of differential operators with constant coefficients on these spaces. In Section 4 we prove our main result on the explicit calculation of Macaulay’s inverse systems of algebras with Gorenstein duality. We also consider two important examples of local algebras and graded algebras with duality. Finally, Section 5 is devoted to the application of our main results to the computation of cohomology rings of toric bundles.

2 Algebras with Gorenstein duality

In this section we study (not-necessarily Artinian) algebras with Gorenstein duality and describe a construction of such algebras recently obtained in [KKE21].

2.1 Algebras with Gorenstein duality

Let 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} be a field of characteristic 00, in this paper we assume 𝐤=ℚ,ℝ{\mathbf{k}}={\mathbb{Q}},{\mathbb{R}} or ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Let AA be a commutative algebra with identity over 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}. A linear function ℓ:A→𝐤\ell\colon A\to{\mathbf{k}} defines a symmetric, bilinear pairing on AA via:

⟨a,b⟩ℓ:=ℓ⁡(a⋅b)​ for any ​a,b∈A.\langle a,b\rangle_{\ell}:=\ell(a\cdot b)\text{ for any }a,b\in A.
Definition 2.1.

A pairing ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℓ\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell} on algebra AA is called Gorenstein duality if it is non-degenerate.

The following lemma gives another characterization of Gorenstein duality.

Lemma 2.2.

Let ℓ:A→𝐤\ell\colon A\to{\mathbf{k}} be any linear function, then

⟨a​b,c⟩ℓ=⟨a,b​c⟩ℓ∀a,b,c∈A.\langle ab,c\rangle_{\ell}=\langle a,bc\rangle_{\ell}\quad\forall a,b,c\in A.

Moreover, any symmetric bilinear pairing ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle such that ⟨a​b,c⟩=⟨a,b​c⟩\langle ab,c\rangle=\langle a,bc\rangle for any a,b,c∈Aa,b,c\in A is given by some linear function.

Proof.

For the first part it is enough to notice that for all a,b,c∈Aa,b,c\in A

⟨a​b,c⟩ℓ=ℓ⁡(a​b​c)=⟨a,b​c⟩ℓ.\langle ab,c\rangle_{\ell}=\ell(abc)=\langle a,bc\rangle_{\ell}.

For the second part, define function ℓ:A→𝐤\ell\colon A\to{\mathbf{k}} via ℓ⁡(a)=⟨1,a⟩\ell(a)=\langle 1,a\rangle. Since ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is symmetric and bilinear, the function ℓ\ell is linear. Moreover, for any a,b∈Aa,b\in A

⟨a,b⟩=⟨1,a​b⟩=ℓ⁡(a​b)=⟨a,b⟩ℓ,\langle a,b\rangle=\langle 1,ab\rangle=\ell(ab)=\langle a,b\rangle_{\ell},

which finishes the proof. ∎

In the case when algebra AA is Artinian, the existence of Gorenstein duality implies that AA is a Gorenstein algebra (in fact these two properties are equivalent). In what follows we will not assume an algebra AA to be Artinian, in this case an algebra with a Gorenstein duality is not necessarily Gorenstein.

Let W⊂AW\subset A be a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space which generates algebra AA multiplicatively, i.e. every element a∈Aa\in A can be represented as a finite sum:

a=P1​(v1,…,vk),a=P_{1}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}),

with vi∈Vv_{i}\in V and P∈𝐤⁡[x1,…,xk]P\in{\mathbf{k}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}] is a polynomial with coefficients in 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}. Let further π:V→W\pi\colon V\to W be a surjective linear map. A map π\pi induces an algebra homomorphism

π:Sym⁡(V)→A,\pi\colon{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A,

which we will denote with the same symbol. Since WW generates algebra AA, the homomorphism π\pi above is surjective. Let ℓ~=ℓ∘π\widetilde{\ell}=\ell\circ\pi be a linear function on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) induced by ℓ\ell. Then the following description of commutative algebras with Gorenstein duality was obtained in [KKE21].

Theorem 2.3 ([KKE21]).

The kernel of the map π:Sym⁡(V)→A\pi\colon{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A is given by

ker⁡(π)={P∈Sym⁡(V)|ℓ~​(P⋅Q)=0​ for any ​Q∈Sym⁡(V)},\ker(\pi)=\{P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\,|\,\widetilde{\ell}(P\cdot Q)=0\text{ for any }Q\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\},

where ℓ~=π∗​ℓ\widetilde{\ell}=\pi^{*}\ell. Moreover, for a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space VV, factor algebras of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) with chosen Gorenstein duality are in bijection with linear functions on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V).

For a linear function ℓ~\widetilde{\ell}, on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V), we will denote by Iℓ~I_{\widetilde{\ell}} the corresponding ideal:

Iℓ~={P∈Sym⁡(V)|ℓ~​(P⋅Q)=0​ for any ​Q∈Sym⁡(V)}I_{\widetilde{\ell}}=\{P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\,|\,\widetilde{\ell}(P\cdot Q)=0\text{ for any }Q\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\}

Theorem 2.3 implies that the classification of algebras with Gorenstein duality boils down to a description of the dual space of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V).

3 Polynomials and formal polynomial series on infinite dimensional vector spaces

In this section we give definitions of polynomial maps and formal polynomial series on an infinite dimensional vector space. We also define an action of symmetric algebra Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) of a vector space VV on the space of polynomial maps and formal polynomial series on VV.

3.1 Polynomial maps between infinite dimensional vector spaces

The notion of polynomial function on infinite dimensional vector space was used by Pukhlikov and the first author, our approach closely follows the one in [PK92a].

Definition 3.1.

We will call a function f:V→𝐤f:V\to{\mathbf{k}} a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd if its restriction to any finite dimensional vector subspace of VV is a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd. A polynomial on VV is a finite sum of homogeneous polynomials.

More generally, we will need a notion of a polynomial map between two (not-necessarily finite dimensional) vector spaces.

Definition 3.2.

A map f:V→Wf:V\to W between two vector spaces is called a polynomial map of degree dd, if for any linear function ℓ∈W∨\ell\in W^{\vee} the composition ℓ∘f:V→𝐤\ell\circ f:V\to{\mathbf{k}} is a polynomial of degree dd.

One has an equivalent definition of a polynomial map between two vector spaces.

Definition 3.3.

A map f:V→Wf:V\to W between two vector spaces is called a polynomial map of degree dd, if for every finite dimensional subspace V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V the image f⁡(V′)f(V^{\prime}) is contained in a finite dimensional subspace W′⊂WW^{\prime}\subset W and the restriction f:V′→W′f:V^{\prime}\to W^{\prime} is a polynomial map of degree dd (in the usual sense).

Lemma 3.4.

Definitions 3.2 and 3.3 of polynomial maps between two vector spaces are equivalent.

Proof.

Assume f:V→Wf:V\to W is a polynomial map in the sense of Definitions 3.3 and let V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V be a finite dimensional vector space. Then the map f:V′→s​p​a​n​(f⁡(V′))f:V^{\prime}\to span(f(V^{\prime})) is a polynomial map between two finite dimensional vector spaces and, therefore, ϕ∘f\phi\circ f is a polynomial on V′V^{\prime} for any ϕ∈W∨\phi\in W^{\vee}.

For the other direction assume f:V→Wf:V\to W is a polynomial map in the sense of Definitions 3.2 and let V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V be a finite dimensional vector space. First we will show that W′=s​p​a​n​(f⁡(V′))W^{\prime}=span(f(V^{\prime})) is finite. Indeed, since for any linear function ϕ∈W∨\phi\in W^{\vee}, the compositions ϕ∘f\phi\circ f is a polynomial on V′V^{\prime} of degree less or equal to dd, we have a linear map:

(W′)∨→Sym≤d​((V′)∨).(W^{\prime})^{\vee}\to{\mathrm{Sym}}_{\leq d}\left((V^{\prime})^{\vee}\right).

Moreover, since W′=s​p​a​n​(f⁡(V′))W^{\prime}=span(f(V^{\prime})), the map above is injective, and hence dimW′≤dimSym≤d​((V′)∨)<∞\dim W^{\prime}\leq\dim{\mathrm{Sym}}_{\leq d}\left((V^{\prime})^{\vee}\right)<\infty. The restriction f:V′→W′f:V^{\prime}\to W^{\prime} is polynomial since its composition with coordinate functions (with respect to any basis of W′W^{\prime}) are polynomials. ∎

The following construction of the polynomial mappings will be very important for this paper. Let VV be a vector space over 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} and let P=a0+a1​x+…+an​xn∈𝐤⁡[x]P=a_{0}+a_{1}x+\ldots+a_{n}x^{n}\in{\mathbf{k}}[x] be a univariate polynomial. Then there is a polynomial mapping P~:V→Sym⁡(V)\widetilde{P}:V\to{\mathrm{Sym}}(V) defined via:

P~​(v)=a0+a1​v+…+an​vn∈Sym⁡(V)\widetilde{P}(v)=a_{0}+a_{1}v+\ldots+a_{n}v^{n}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)

The Example 3.5 below is a slight generalisation of this construction.

Example 3.5.

Let AA be an algebra with identity and ϕ:V→A\phi\colon V\to A be a linear map. Then every univariate polynomial P=a0+a1​x+…+an​xn∈A⁡[x]P=a_{0}+a_{1}x+\ldots+a_{n}x^{n}\in A[x] with coefficients in AA defines a polynomial mapping V→AV\to A via

P~​(v)=a0+a1​ϕ​(v)+a2​ϕ​(v)2+…+an​ϕ​(v)n∈A.\widetilde{P}(v)=a_{0}+a_{1}\phi(v)+a_{2}\phi(v)^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}\phi(v)^{n}\in A.

In particular, every polynomial P∈𝐤⁡[x]P\in{\mathbf{k}}[x] with coefficients in 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} defines a polynomial map P~:V→A\widetilde{P}:V\to A.

3.2 Action of symmetric algebra on the space of polynomial maps

For a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space VV we denote by Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) its symmetric algebra, i.e. the quotient of tensor algebra of VV by two-sided ideal generated by elements of the form v⊗w−w⊗vv\otimes w-w\otimes v. We identify Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) with the space Diff⁡(V){\mathrm{Diff}}(V) of differential operators with constant coefficients on VV in the following way. The zero degree component Sym0​(V)≃𝐤{\mathrm{Sym}}_{0}(V)\simeq{\mathbf{k}} corresponds to operators of multiplication by a number. For elements of positive degree we define the map

𝒟:v1​…​vk↦Lv1​…​Lvk,\mathcal{D}\colon v_{1}\ldots v_{k}\mapsto L_{v_{1}}\ldots L_{v_{k}},

where LvL_{v} is the Gateaux derivative in the direction v∈Vv\in V. For a map f:V→Wf:V\to W its Gateaux derivative in the direction v∈Vv\in V is given by

Lv​f​(x)=limt→0f⁡(x+t​v)−f⁡(x)t,L_{v}f(x)=\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t}, (1)

if the limit exists ([Gat19]).

Remark 3.6.

For a general map f:V→Wf:V\to W for the limit on the right had side of (1) to be defined, one need to choose a topology on the target vector space WW. In this paper we would work with polynomial mappings, so for fixed vv and xx, the image f⁡(x+t​v)f(x+tv) always belong to a finite dimensional subspace of WW and hence the limit limt→0f⁡(x+t​v)−f⁡(x)t\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t} is well defined. In other words, we endow WW with the topology for which a subset U⊂WU\subset W is open if and only if U∩W′U\cap W^{\prime} is open for every finite dimensional vector subspace W′⊂WW^{\prime}\subset W.

Remark 3.7.

Since for the computation of the value of the Gateaux derivative Lv​f​(x)L_{v}f(x) of a polynomial mapping at a fixed point x∈Vx\in V we need to work with only finite dimensional vector spaces, we can define the Gateaux derivative purely formally. This allows to extend all our results to any field 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} of characteristic 00.

For an element P∈Sym⁡(V)P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V), we denote by 𝒟P{\mathcal{D}}_{P} the corresponding differential operator. It is easy to check that for a polynomial map f:V→Wf:V\to W of degree dd and a vector v∈Vv\in V, the Gateaux derivative Lv​fL_{v}f is a polynomial map of degree d−1d-1 or 0. Therefore, the space of polynomial mappings has a structure of a graded module over Diff⁡(V){\mathrm{Diff}}(V).

Example 3.8.

Let f:V→𝐤f:V\to{\mathbf{k}} be a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd, then for any v∈Vv\in V, we have 𝒟vd⋅f:=(Lv)d⋅f≡d!​f​(v){\mathcal{D}}_{v^{d}}\cdot f:=(L_{v})^{d}\cdot f\equiv d!f(v) is a constant function.

Example 3.9 (Continuation of Example 3.5).

Let AA be an algebra with identity and ϕ:V→A\phi\colon V\to A be a linear map. Let P~\widetilde{P} be a polynomial map P~:V→A\widetilde{P}:V\to A given by a univariate polynomial P∈A⁡[x]P\in A[x]. Let further v∈Vv\in V be a vector, then one has

Lv​P~=ϕ⁡(v)⋅∂xP~,L_{v}\widetilde{P}=\phi(v)\cdot\widetilde{\partial_{x}P},

where ∂xP~\widetilde{\partial_{x}P} is a polynomial map given by the usual derivative ∂xP\partial_{x}P of PP. By linearity, it is enough to check the formula above for P=ai​xiP=a_{i}x^{i} being a monomial in A⁡[x]A[x]. So we have:

Lv⋅(ai​xi~)=limt→0ai⋅ϕ​(x+t​v)i−ai⋅ϕ​(x)it=limt→0ai⋅(ϕ⁡(x)+t​ϕ​(v))i−ϕ​(x)it=ai⋅ϕ⁡(v)⋅i​ϕ​(x)i−1.L_{v}\cdot(\widetilde{a_{i}x^{i}})=\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{a_{i}\cdot\phi(x+tv)^{i}-a_{i}\cdot\phi(x)^{i}}{t}=\lim_{t\to 0}a_{i}\cdot\frac{(\phi(x)+t\phi(v))^{i}-\phi(x)^{i}}{t}=a_{i}\cdot\phi(v)\cdot i\phi(x)^{i-1}.

3.3 Formal polynomial series

In this subsection we introduce a more general notion of formal polynomial series and formal polynomial series with values in a vector space WW.

Definition 3.10.

For (not-necessarily finite dimensional) vector spaces VV and WW, a formal polynomial series on VV with values in WW is a formal sum

f=f0+f1+…+fi+…,f=f_{0}+f_{1}+\ldots+f_{i}+\ldots,

where fi:V→Wf_{i}:V\to W is a homogeneous polynomial map of degree ii. A formal polynomial series with values in 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} is just called a formal polynomial series.

We can extend the action of Diff⁡(V){\mathrm{Diff}}(V) on the space of formal polynomial series 𝐤​⟦V⟧{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket via term-wise differentiation:

𝒟P​(∑i=0∞fi)=∑i=r∞𝒟P​(fi),{\mathcal{D}}_{P}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}f_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=r}^{\infty}{\mathcal{D}}_{P}(f_{i}),

for a homogeneous polynomial P∈Symr​(V)P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}_{r}(V) extended by linearity for general P∈Sym⁡(V)P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V). For a formal polynomial series F=∑i=0∞fiF=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}f_{i}, let us denote by F⁡(0)F(0) its constant term f0∈𝐤f_{0}\in{\mathbf{k}}.

As in the case of polynomial maps, in this paper we are mostly interested in the following special class of formal polynomial series.

Example 3.11 (Continuation of Example 3.5).

As before, let AA be an algebra with identity and ϕ:V→A\phi\colon V\to A be a linear map. Then every univariate formal power series f=∑i=0∞ai​xi∈A⁡⟦x⟧f=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}x^{i}\in A\llbracket x\rrbracket with coefficients in AA defines a formal polynomial series on VV with values in AA via

f~=a0+a1​ϕ​(v)+a2​ϕ​(v)2+…+an​ϕ​(v)n+….\widetilde{f}=a_{0}+a_{1}\phi(v)+a_{2}\phi(v)^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}\phi(v)^{n}+\ldots.

Note that each summand in the expression above is indeed a homogeneous polynomial mapping from VV to AA, so their (formal) sum is a formal polynomial series with values in AA.

In particular, every formal power series every polynomial f∈𝐤​⟦x⟧f\in{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket x\rrbracket with coefficients in 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} defines a polynomial map P~:V→A\widetilde{P}:V\to A.

As before, the action of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) on formal polynomial series as in Example 3.11 has an easy description.

Proposition 3.12.

Let AA be an algebra and ϕ:V→A\phi\colon V\to A be a 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}-linear map. Let f~\widetilde{f} be a formal polynomial series with values in AA given by a univariate power series f⁡(x)=∑i=0∞ai​xif(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}x^{i} with ai∈Aa_{i}\in A. Then for any v∈Vv\in V, we have

Lv​f~=ϕ⁡(v)⋅∂xf~,L_{v}\widetilde{f}=\phi(v)\cdot\widetilde{\partial_{x}f},

where ∂xf~\widetilde{\partial_{x}f} is the formal polynomial series with values in AA given by the derivative ∂xf\partial_{x}f of ff.

Proof.

Since we apply the differentiation to f~\widetilde{f} term-wise, it is enough to show that Lv​(ai​ϕ​(x)i)=ϕ⁡(v)⋅i​ai​ϕ​(x)i−1L_{v}(a_{i}\phi(x)^{i})=\phi(v)\cdot ia_{i}\phi(x)^{i-1}, which was done in Example 3.9. ∎

As an immediate corollary, we obtain the following statement, which is the central part of this section.

Corollary 3.13.

Let AA be an algebra and ϕ:V→A\phi\colon V\to A be a 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}-linear map. Let Exp⁡(x){\mathrm{Exp}}(x) be a formal polynomial series with values in AA given by a exponential power series ∑i=0∞xii!\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{i}}{i!}. Then for any P∈Sym⁡(V)P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)

𝒟P⋅Exp⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(P)⋅Exp⁡(x).{\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}(x)=\phi(P)\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}(x).
Proof.

The statement follows from successive application of Proposition 3.12 and the fact that the derivative of the exponential power series is itself. ∎

Let us denote by 𝐤​⟦V⟧{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket the space of formal polynomial series on VV. Given a formal polynomial series ff on VV with values in WW, one can pullback the linear functions on WW to formal polynomial series on VV. In other words one has a map:

f∗:W∨→𝐤⁡⟦V⟧,ℓ↦ℓ∘f0+ℓ∘f1+…f^{*}:W^{\vee}\to{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket,\quad\ell\mapsto\ell\circ f_{0}+\ell\circ f_{1}+\ldots

By Definition 3.2 each of the compositions ℓ∘fi\ell\circ f_{i} is a homogeneous polynomial of degree ii, so the sum on the right hand side is indeed a formal polynomial series.

We finish this section with the proof that the space of formal polynomial series is isomorphic to the dual vector space to symmetric algebra Sym​(V)∨{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee}. First we will need the following definition.

Definition 3.14.

Define a bilinear pairing BB between Diff⁡(V){\mathrm{Diff}}(V) (≃Sym⁡(V)\simeq{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)) and 𝐤​⟦V⟧{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket in the following way

⟨𝒟P,F⟩:=(𝒟P⋅F)​(0),\langle{\mathcal{D}}_{P},F\rangle:=({\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot F)(0),

where (𝒟P⋅F)​(0)({\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot F)(0) as before denotes the constant term of a formal polynomial series.

The pairing from Definition 3.14 defines a map B:𝐤⁡⟦V⟧→Sym​(V)∨B:{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket\to{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee} via f↦⟨⋅,f⟩.f\mapsto\langle\cdot,f\rangle.

Theorem 3.15.

Let VV be a vector space and let as before, Exp{\mathrm{Exp}} be a formal polynomial map with values in Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) given by the exponential power series. Then the map

Exp∗:Sym​(V)∨→𝐤⁡⟦V⟧{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}:{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee}\to{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket

is the inverse of the map B:𝐤⁡⟦V⟧→Sym​(V)∨B:{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket\to{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee} induced by the pairing in Definition 3.14. In particular, both maps are isomorphisms of vector spaces.

Proof.

Since both maps are linear, it is enough to check that Exp∗∘B:𝐤⁡⟦V⟧→𝐤⁡⟦V⟧{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}\circ B\colon{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket\to{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket is identity. This follows from a direct computation and Example 3.8. Indeed let f=∑i=0∞fif=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}f_{i} be a formal polynomial series, then

(Exp∗∘B)​(f)=∑i=0∞𝒟xii!⋅f⁡(0)=∑i=0∞𝒟xii!⋅fi=∑i=0∞fi​(x)=f.\left({\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}\circ B\right)(f)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{\mathcal{D}}_{\frac{x^{i}}{i!}}\cdot f(0)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{\mathcal{D}}_{\frac{x^{i}}{i!}}\cdot f_{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}f_{i}(x)=f.

∎

Corollary 3.16.

For a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space VV, factor algebras of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) with chosen Gorenstein duality are in bijection with formal polynomial series on VV.

Proof.

Statement follows from Theorem 2.3 and the fact that Sym​(V)∨≃𝐤⁡⟦V⟧{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee}\simeq{\mathbf{k}}\llbracket V\rrbracket. ∎

Another immediate corollary of Theorem 3.15 is the following statement.

Corollary 3.17.

For any linear function ℓ∈Sym​(V)∨\ell\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee} we have

ℓ⁡(P)=⟨𝒟P,Exp∗​(ℓ)⟩,\ell(P)=\langle{\mathcal{D}}_{P},{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}(\ell)\rangle,

where Exp{\mathrm{Exp}} is the exponential formal polynomial series with values in Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V).

4 Explicit description of Macaulay’s inverse system

In this subsection we obtain an explicit description of Macaulay’s inverse system for algebras with Gorenstein duality over field of characteristic 00. First we need the following lemma.

Lemma 4.1.

Let ℓ~∈Sym​(V)∨\widetilde{\ell}\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)^{\vee} be a linear function on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V). Then the ideal Iℓ~I_{\widetilde{\ell}} coincides with

Ann⁡(Exp∗​ℓ~)={P∈Sym⁡(V)|𝒟P⋅Exp∗​ℓ~=0}.{\mathrm{Ann}}({\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}})=\{P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\,|\,{\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}=0\}.
Proof.

If P∈Ann⁡(Exp∗​ℓ~)P\in{\mathrm{Ann}}({\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}), then ℓ~​(Q⋅P)=⟨Q⋅P,Exp∗​ℓ~⟩=0\widetilde{\ell}(Q\cdot P)=\langle Q\cdot P,{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}\rangle=0, for any Q∈Sym⁡(V)Q\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V). Hence P∈Iℓ~P\in I_{\widetilde{\ell}}.

For the other direction, notice that if 𝒟P⋅Exp∗​ℓ~≠0{\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}\neq 0, then there exists at least one non-zero component of 𝒟P⋅Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}, and therefore there exist QQ such that the constant term of 𝒟Q⋅P⋅Exp∗​ℓ~=𝒟Q⋅𝒟p⋅Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathcal{D}}_{Q\cdot P}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}={\mathcal{D}}_{Q}\cdot{\mathcal{D}}_{p}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} is non zero. Thus if P∉Ann⁡(Exp∗​ℓ~)P\notin{\mathrm{Ann}}({\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}), we also have P∉Iℓ~P\notin I_{\widetilde{\ell}}. ∎

Now we are ready to give a construction of algebras with Gorenstein duality. As before, let AA be a commutative algebra, ℓ\ell be a linear function on AA which induces a non-degenerate pairing ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℓ\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell}. Let further W⊂AW\subset A be a vector subspace which generates AA multiplicatively and let π:V→W\pi:V\to W be a surjective linear mapping. The immediate corollary of Theorem 2.3 and Lemma 4.1 is the following theorem.

Theorem 4.2.

Let AA be a commutative algebra over 𝐤{\mathbf{k}} with Gorenstein duality given by linear function ℓ:A→𝐤\ell:A\to{\mathbf{k}}. Let VV be a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space and let π:Sym⁡(V)→A\pi:{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A be surjection. Then we have

A≃Sym⁡(V)/Ann⁡(Exp∗​ℓ~),A\simeq{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)/{\mathrm{Ann}}({\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}),

where Ann⁡(Exp∗​ℓ~)={P∈Sym⁡(V)|𝒟P⋅Exp∗​ℓ~=0}{\mathrm{Ann}}({\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}})=\{P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\,|\,{\mathcal{D}}_{P}\cdot{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}=0\}.

For an algebra AA with duality given by linear function ℓ\ell and a surjection π:Sym⁡(V)→A\pi:{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A, we will call the formal polynomial series Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} the potential of AA with respect to the generating space VV.

4.1 Graded algebras with Gorenstein duality

In this subsection we consider important partial cases of algebras with Gorenstein duality whose potentials are actual polynomials.

Let AA be a local algebra with maximal ideal 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} and the residue field A/𝔪≃𝐤A/{\mathfrak{m}}\simeq{\mathbf{k}} with duality defined by a function ℓ\ell. Assume further that 𝔪d=0{\mathfrak{m}}^{d}=0 for some dd. Let W⊂𝔪W\subset{\mathfrak{m}} be a subspace which generates AA multiplicatively and let V→WV\to W be a surjective map.

Proposition 4.3.

For AA and VV as above, the potential Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} of AA on VV has only finitely many non-zero sumands. In over words, Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} is a polynomial on VV.

Proof.

Proposition immediately follows from the fact that π⁡(xi)=0\pi(x^{i})=0 for any x∈Vx\in V and i≥di\geq d. ∎

The most important example of local algebras with Gorenstein duality for us are graded algebras. Let

A=⨁i=0nAi,A=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n}A_{i},

be a commutative graded algebra over 𝐤{\mathbf{k}}, such that

  • •

    A0≃An≃𝐤A_{0}\simeq A_{n}\simeq{\mathbf{k}};

  • •

    the natural bilinear pairing Ai×An−i→An≃kA_{i}\times A_{n-i}\to A_{n}\simeq k is non-degenerate for any i=0,…,ni=0,\ldots,n.

Let us fix an isomorphism ℓ:An≃𝐤\ell:A_{n}\simeq{\mathbf{k}} and extend it to the whole AA trivially, i.e. ℓ⁡(Ai)=0\ell(A_{i})=0, for i≠ni\neq n. Then a function ℓ\ell provides a Gorenstein duality.

Let W⊂AW\subset A be a (possibly infinite dimensional) vector space which contains multiplicative generators of AA. Then WW has a natural structure of a graded vector space:

W=⨁i=0nWi,Wi=W∩Ai.W=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n}W_{i},\quad W_{i}=W\cap A_{i}.

Let further π:V→⨁i=1nWi\pi:V\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}W_{i} be a surjectiction to the subspace of WW of elements of positive degree. One can pullback the grading of WW to a grading of VV:

V=⨁i=1nVi,Vi=π−1​(Wi).V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}V_{i},\quad V_{i}=\pi^{-1}(W_{i}).

As before, the surjection π:V→⨁i=1nWi\pi:V\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}W_{i} extends to a surjective homomorphism of algebras π:Sym⁡(V)→A\pi:{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A. Moreover, the grading on VV defines a grading on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) via

deg⁡(v1k1​…​vnkn)=∑i=1ni​ki,\deg\left(v_{1}^{k_{1}}\ldots v_{n}^{k_{n}}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}ik_{i}, (2)

for any vi∈Viv_{i}\in V_{i}. This grading on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) makes the homomorphism π:Sym⁡(V)→A\pi\colon{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A graded. Let

Sym⁡(V)=⨁i=0∞Symi​(V),{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\infty}{\mathrm{Sym}}_{i}(V),

be a decomposition into quasi-homogeneous components (i.e. homogeneous with respect to the grading from (2)). We will say that a linear function ℓ~:Sym⁡(V)→𝐤\widetilde{\ell}:{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to{\mathbf{k}} is nn quasi-homogeneous if

ℓ~​(Symi​(V))=0, for ​i≠n.\widetilde{\ell}({\mathrm{Sym}}_{i}(V))=0,\text{ for }i\neq n.
Theorem 4.4.

Let VV be a (possibly infinite dimensional) graded vector space. Then graded Gorenstein factor algebras of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) are in bijection with quasi-homogeneous linear functions on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) up to scaling.

Proof.

Let π:Sym⁡(V)→A\pi:{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\to A be a surjection to a graded algebra A=⨁i=0nAiA=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n}A_{i} with duality and let ℓ:An→𝐤\ell:A_{n}\to{\mathbf{k}}, be some isomorphism (which is unique up to scaling). Then ℓ~=ℓ∘π\widetilde{\ell}=\ell\circ\pi is an nn quasi-homogeneous linear function, and by Theorem 2.3, we have

A≃Sym⁡(V)/Iℓ~.A\simeq{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)/I_{\widetilde{\ell}}.

For the other direction let ℓ~\widetilde{\ell} be an nn quasi-homogeneous linear function on Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V). We will show that the ideal Iℓ~I_{\widetilde{\ell}} is quasi-homogeneous and hence the factor algebra Sym⁡(V)/Iℓ~{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)/I_{\widetilde{\ell}} is a graded Gorenstein algebra.

Let P∈Iℓ~P\in I_{\widetilde{\ell}}, i.e. ℓ~​(P⋅Q)\widetilde{\ell}(P\cdot Q) for any Q∈Sym⁡(V)Q\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V). Let P=∑i=0kPiP=\sum_{i=0}^{k}P_{i} be a decomposition of PP into quasi homogeneous components. Then for any Q∈Sym⁡(V)Q\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V), we have

ℓ~​(Pi⋅Q)=∑jℓ~​(Pi⋅Qj)=ℓ~​(Pi⋅Qn−i),\widetilde{\ell}(P_{i}\cdot Q)=\sum_{j}\widetilde{\ell}(P_{i}\cdot Q_{j})=\widetilde{\ell}(P_{i}\cdot Q_{n-i}),

where Q=∑jQjQ=\sum_{j}Q_{j} is the decomposition into quasi-homogeneous components. But since P∈Iℓ~P\in I_{\widetilde{\ell}} and ℓ~\widetilde{\ell} is nn quasi-homogeneous we have

0=ℓ~​(P⋅Qn−i)=ℓ~​(Pi⋅Qn−i).0=\widetilde{\ell}(P\cdot Q_{n-i})=\widetilde{\ell}(P_{i}\cdot Q_{n-i}).

Thus ℓ~​(Pi⋅Q)=0\widetilde{\ell}(P_{i}\cdot Q)=0 for any Q∈Sym⁡(V)Q\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V) and the ideal Iℓ~I_{\widetilde{\ell}} is quasi-homogeneous. ∎

Now we will give a second version of Theorem 4.4 in terms of potentials. First we will need the following definition.

Definition 4.5.

We will call a function f:V→𝐤f\colon V\to{\mathbf{k}} on a graded vector space a quasi-homogeneous polynomial of degree dd if its restriction to any finite dimensional vector subspace WW of VV which decomposes into graded components is a quasi-homogeneous polynomial of degree dd.

In case when V=V1V=V_{1} is a graded vector space with trivial graded structure, quasi homogeneous polynomials on VV are just homogeneous polynomials. In general we would need the following technical lemma.

Lemma 4.6.

Let VV be a graded vector space, and let f:V→𝐤f\colon V\to{\mathbf{k}} be quasi-homogeneous polynomial. Then ff is a polynomial.

Proof.

It is enough to show that for every finite dimensional W⊂VW\subset V the restriction of ff to WW is a polynomial. But for every such WW one can construct a finite dimensional decomposable W~⊂V\widetilde{W}\subset V with W⊂W~W\subset\widetilde{W}. Since the restriction of ff to W~\widetilde{W} is a polynomial, such is its restriction to WW. ∎

Lemma 4.7.

Let ℓ~\widetilde{\ell} be an nn quasi-homogeneous linear function. Then the formal polynomial series Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} is a quasi-homogeneous polynomial of degree nn.

Proof.

Let V′=⨁i=1nVi′V^{\prime}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}V_{i}^{\prime} be a finite dimensional subspace of VV. Then for an element v=∑viv=\sum v_{i} with vi∈Vi′v_{i}\in V_{i}^{\prime} we have

Exp∗​ℓ~​(v)=∑j=0∞ℓ~​((v1+…+vn)jj!).{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}(v)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\widetilde{\ell}\left(\frac{(v_{1}+\ldots+v_{n})^{j}}{j!}\right).

But since ℓ~\widetilde{\ell} is an nn quasi-homogeneous linear function we have

Exp∗​ℓ~​(v)=∑∑i​ki=nℓ~​(v1k1​…​vnknk1!​…​kn!),{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}(v)=\sum_{\sum ik_{i}=n}\widetilde{\ell}\left(\frac{v_{1}^{k_{1}}\ldots v_{n}^{k_{n}}}{k_{1}!\ldots k_{n}!}\right),

and in particular Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} is a finite sum of quasi-homogeneous polynomials of degree nn. ∎

Now we are ready to formulate the main result of this subsection.

Theorem 4.8.

Let VV be a (possibly infinite dimensional) graded vector space. Then graded factor algebras of Sym⁡(V){\mathrm{Sym}}(V) with Gorenstein duality are in bijection with quasi-homogeneous polynomials on VV. For a quasi-homogeneous polynomial ff, the corresponding algebra is given by

A=Sym⁡(V)/Ann⁡(f),A={\mathrm{Sym}}(V)/{\mathrm{Ann}}(f),

Where Ann⁡(f)={P∈Sym⁡(V)|𝒟P​(f)=0}{\mathrm{Ann}}(f)=\{P\in{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)\,|\,{\mathcal{D}}_{P}(f)=0\}.

Proof.

Theorem follows immediately from Theorem 4.4 and Lemmas 4.1, 4.7. ∎

Example 4.9.

Let algebra A=⨁i=0nAiA=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n}A_{i} be as before. Assume further that AA is generated in degree 1, and V→A1V\to A_{1} is a surjective map. Then the potential Exp∗​ℓ~{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}} of AA on VV is given by

Exp∗​ℓ~​(v)=ℓ~​(vnn!).{\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}{\widetilde{\ell}}(v)=\widetilde{\ell}\left(\frac{v^{n}}{n!}\right).

In particular algebra AA can be constructed as

A≃Diff⁡(A)/Ann⁡(ℓ~​(vnn!)).A\simeq{\mathrm{Diff}}(A)/{\mathrm{Ann}}\left(\widetilde{\ell}\left(\frac{v^{n}}{n!}\right)\right).

The result from Example 4.9 was observed in [PK92b] where it was applied to the computation of cohomology ring of toric varieties. It was also used in [Kav11] for the computation of the cohomology rings of full flag varieties G/BG/B and in [KK20] for the computation of the ring of complete intersections of an algebraic variety. These results crucially use that the above rings are generated in degree 1 (after dividing grading by 22 for cohomology rings).

5 Potential of a toric bundle

In this section we will apply our explicit version of Macaulay’s inverse system to the computation of the ring of even degree cohomology classes of toric bundles. In particular, we obtain complete description of cohomology rings of toroidal horospherical varieties and the ring of conditions of horospherical homogeneous spaces.

5.1 Virtual polytopes and cohomology ring of a toric variety

In this subsection we briefly recall the relation of the space of virtual polytopes to the cohomology rings of toric varieties. For more detailed background on virtual polytopes we refer to [PS15]. We also refer to [CLS11] for the introduction to toric geometry.

Let T≃(ℂ∗)nT\simeq({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{n} be an algebraic torus with a character lattice MM and a cocharacter lattice N:=Hom⁡(M,ℤ)N:={\mathrm{Hom}}(M,{\mathbb{Z}}). Let Mℝ:=M⊗ℝM_{\mathbb{R}}:=M\otimes{\mathbb{R}} and Nℝ:=N⊗ℝN_{\mathbb{R}}:=N\otimes{\mathbb{R}} be the corresponding vector spaces.

Let us denote by 𝒫+{\mathcal{P}}^{+} the set of all convex polytopes in MℝM_{\mathbb{R}}. Note that 𝒫+{\mathcal{P}}^{+} is a cone with respect the Minkowski addition and scaling by a positive factor. Moreover, 𝒫+{\mathcal{P}}^{+} has the cancellation property, i.e.

Δ1+Δ=Δ2+Δif and only ifΔ1=Δ2.\Delta_{1}+\Delta=\Delta_{2}+\Delta\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}.

Thus we can consider a Grothendieck group associated to 𝒫+{\mathcal{P}}^{+}.

Definition 5.1.

The space of virtual polytopes 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} is the Grothendieck group of the semigroup of convex polytopes 𝒫+{\mathcal{P}}^{+}.

Let us fix a complete fan Σ⊂N\Sigma\subset N which is a normal fan of some polytope. Let further 𝒫Σ+{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}^{+} be the set of polytopes in MℝM_{\mathbb{R}} such that Σ\Sigma refines their normal fans. It is easy to see that 𝒫Σ+{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}^{+} is a subsemigroup of 𝒫Σ{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}. Similar to the general case, the space of virtual polytopes 𝒫Σ{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} associated with fan Σ\Sigma is the Grothendieck group of the semigroup of convex polytopes 𝒫Σ+{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}^{+}.

The scaling by positive real numbers of convex polytopes 𝒫Σ+{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}^{+} extends to the action of ℝ{\mathbb{R}} on 𝒫Σ{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}, making it into a vector space. In what follows we will use a more concrete description of 𝒫Σ{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}. Using support functions, one can identify 𝒫Σ+{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}^{+} with a cone of convex, piecewise linear function on NℝN_{\mathbb{R}} which are linear on all cones of Σ\Sigma. This identification extends to the space of virtual polytopes, and since any piecewise linear function is a difference of two convex piecewise linear functions, we have

𝒫Σ={h:Nℝ→ℝ:piecewise linear function onΣ}.{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}=\{h\colon N_{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}\colon\text{piecewise linear function on}\;\Sigma\}.

In particular, the description above allows to work with the spaces of virtual polytopes associated to fans Σ\Sigma which are not normal for any polytope.

Similarly, the space of all virtual polytopes 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} can be identified with all functions h:Nℝ→ℝh\colon N_{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} which are piecewise linear with respect to some fan Σ\Sigma. For a virtual polytope Δ∈𝒫\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}, we will call the corresponding piecewise linear function hΔ:Nℝ→ℝh_{\Delta}\colon N_{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} the support function of Δ\Delta.

For an integral fan Σ⊂Nℝ\Sigma\subset N_{\mathbb{R}}, let us denote by YΣY_{\Sigma} the corresponding toric variety. We will say that Σ\Sigma is a smooth projective fan if the corresponding toric variety is such.

Each virtual polytope Δ∈𝒫Σ\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} defines a degree two cohomology class on a toric variety YΣY_{\Sigma} in the following way. Let e1,…,ere_{1},\ldots,e_{r} be the integral ray generators of Σ\Sigma and D1,…,DrD_{1},\ldots,D_{r} be the corresponding TT-invariant divisors on YΣY_{\Sigma}. Let further hΔ:Nℝ→ℝh_{\Delta}:N_{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} be the support function of a (virtual) polytope Δ\Delta. Then we have a map

𝒫Σ→H2​(YΣ,ℝ),Δ↦∑hΔ​(ei)​[Di],{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\to H^{2}(Y_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}}),\quad\Delta\mapsto\sum h_{\Delta}(e_{i})[D_{i}],

where [Di]∈H2​(YΣ)[D_{i}]\in H^{2}(Y_{\Sigma}) is a class Poincaré dual to the homology class of the divisor DiD_{i}.

The following theorem is well-known (see, for example, [CLS11]).

Theorem 5.2.

The map 𝒫Σ→H2​(YΣ,ℝ){\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\to H^{2}(Y_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}}) is surjective. Moreover, H∗​(YΣ,ℝ)H^{*}(Y_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}}) is generated in degree 2, thus one has a surjective ring homomorphism:

Sym⁡(𝒫Σ)→H∗​(YΣ,ℝ).{\mathrm{Sym}}({\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma})\to H^{*}(Y_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}}).

5.2 Preliminaries on toric bundles

In this subsection we give preliminaries on toric bundles, for more detailed treatment see Section 3 of [HKM20].

Let TT be an algebraic torus as before and let E→XE\to X be a TT-principle bundle over smooth closed orientable manifold. For any manifold YY with a continuous action by TT let E×TY≔(E×Y)/TE\times_{T}Y\coloneqq(E\times Y)/T be the associated fiber bundle over XX. It is easy to see that a fiber of the bundle E×TY→XE\times_{T}Y\to X is homeomorphic to YY.

For any λ∈Y\lambda\in Y, let ℂλ{\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda} be the corresponding 1-dimensional representation of TT and let ℒλ:=E×Tℂλ{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}:=E\times_{T}{\mathbb{C}}_{\lambda} be the associated complex line bundle over XX. One can see that

ℒλ+μ=ℒλ⊗ℒμ, for any ​λ,μ∈M.{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda+\mu}={\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}\otimes{\mathcal{L}}_{\mu},\text{ for any }\lambda,\mu\in M.

Thus we have a homomorphism c:M→H2​(X,ℤ)c\colon M\to H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Z}}) of abelian groups defined via

λ↦c1​(ℒλ),\lambda\mapsto c_{1}({\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}),

where c1​(ℒλ)c_{1}({\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}) is the first Chern class of the line bundle ℒλ{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}. We extend the group homomorphism cc to a linear map

c:Mℝ→H2​(X,ℝ).c\colon M_{\mathbb{R}}\to H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}}).

Let Σ⊂N\Sigma\subset N be a smooth, projective fan and let be YΣY_{\Sigma} the corresponding toric variety. We denote by EΣ→XE_{\Sigma}\to X the associated toric bundle:

EΣ=E×TYΣ.E_{\Sigma}=E\times_{T}Y_{\Sigma}.

The following result describes the cohomology groups of a toric bundle. It is an easy corollary of Leray-Hirsch theorem ([BT82, Theorem 5.11]).

Proposition 5.3.

Let TT be an algebraic torus, p:E→Xp\colon E\to X be a TT-principle bundle, and YΣY_{\Sigma} be a smooth projective TT–toric variety given by a fan Σ\Sigma. Then as a group the cohomology of EΣ=E×TYΣE_{\Sigma}=E\times_{T}Y_{\Sigma} is given by

H∗​(EΣ,ℝ)≃H∗​(X,ℝ)⊗H∗​(YΣ,ℝ)​.H^{*}(E_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}})\simeq H^{*}(X,{\mathbb{R}})\otimes H^{*}(Y_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}})\text{.} (3)

As before, to each virtual polytope Δ∈𝒫Σ\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} we can associate a degree 2 cohomology in H2​(YΣ,ℝ)H^{2}(Y_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}}). thus, using isomorphism (3), to each virtual polytope Δ∈𝒫Σ\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} we can associate a degree 2 cohomology class on the corresponding toric bundle EΣE_{\Sigma}:

ρ:𝒫Σ→H2​(EΣ),Δ↦∑1⊗hΔ​(ei)​[Di]∈H∗​(X)⊗H∗​(YΣ)≃H∗​(EΣ).\rho\colon{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\to H^{2}(E_{\Sigma}),\quad\Delta\mapsto\sum 1\otimes h_{\Delta}(e_{i})[D_{i}]\in H^{*}(X)\otimes H^{*}(Y_{\Sigma})\simeq H^{*}(E_{\Sigma}).

Moreover we have the following proposition

Proposition 5.4.

The cohomology ring of a toric bundle p:EΣ→Xp:E_{\Sigma}\to X is generated by the image of H∗​(X,ℝ)⊕𝒫ΣH^{*}(X,{\mathbb{R}})\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} under

p∗⊕ρ:H∗​(X,ℝ)⊕𝒫Σ→H∗​(EΣ,ℝ).p^{*}\oplus\rho\colon H^{*}(X,{\mathbb{R}})\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\to H^{*}(E_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}}).
Proof.

The proposition follows immediately from Theorem 5.2 and Proposition 5.3. ∎

5.3 Potential on toric bundles

In this section we assume that dimℝX=2​k\dim_{\mathbb{R}}X=2k is even. In that case, dimℝEΣ=2​k+2​n\dim_{\mathbb{R}}E_{\Sigma}=2k+2n is also even.

For a manifold MM of even dimension, let us denote by A∗​(Y)A^{*}(Y) the subring of even degree cohomology classes with degrees divided by 2:

A∗​(Y):=⨁i=0(dimℝY)/2H2​i​(Y,ℝ).A^{*}(Y):=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{(\dim_{\mathbb{R}}Y)/2}H^{2i}(Y,{\mathbb{R}}).

The ring A∗​(Y)A^{*}(Y) is a commutative ring with a Gorenstein duality given in the following way. For a manifold YY, we will denote by ℓY:A∗​(Y)→ℝ\ell_{Y}:A^{*}(Y)\to{\mathbb{R}} the linear functional given by the pairing with the fundamental class of YY. That is

ℓY​(γ)=∫Yγ, for ​γ∈A∗​(Y).\ell_{Y}(\gamma)=\int_{Y}\gamma,\quad\text{ for }\gamma\in A^{*}(Y).

By Poincaré duality, the function ℓY\ell_{Y} provides a Gorenstein duality on A∗​(Y)A^{*}(Y) when dimℝ(Y)\dim_{\mathbb{R}}(Y) is even.

Now let E→XE\to X be a TT-principle bundle over smooth closed orientable manifold XX of even dimension 2​k2k. Let further Σ⊂N\Sigma\subset N be a smooth projective fan, and let p:EΣ→Xp:E_{\Sigma}\to X be the corresponding toric bundle. Similar to Proposition 5.4, the ring of even cohomologies A∗​(EΣ)A^{*}(E_{\Sigma}) is generated by the image of A∗​(X)⊕𝒫ΣA^{*}(X)\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} under p∗⊕ρp^{*}\oplus\rho. Thus we have the surjection:

Sym⁡(A∗​(X)⊕𝒫Σ)→A∗​(EΣ).{\mathrm{Sym}}(A^{*}(X)\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma})\to A^{*}(E_{\Sigma}).

We will describe the kernel of the above surjection using the explicit computation of Macaulay’s inverse system given in Theorem 4.2 and a version of the BKK theorem for toric bundles obtained in [HKM20].

First we will need some definitions. For a virtual polytope Δ∈𝒫Σ\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}, define its ii-th horizontal part hi​(Δ)h_{i}(\Delta) to be the unique class in A∗​(X)A^{*}(X) such that

∫EΣρ​(Δ)n+i⋅p∗​(η)=∫Xhi​(Δ)⋅η​,\int_{E_{\Sigma}}\rho(\Delta)^{n+i}\cdot p^{*}(\eta)=\int_{X}h_{i}(\Delta)\cdot\eta\text{,}

for any η∈A∗​(X,ℝ)\eta\in A^{*}(X,{\mathbb{R}}). It is clear that hi​(Δ)h_{i}(\Delta) is a homogeneous element of degree i−ni-n in A∗​(X)A^{*}(X). In particular, hi​(Δ)=0h_{i}(\Delta)=0 for i<ni<n. The horizontal parts of Δ\Delta were computed in [HKM20].

Theorem 5.5 ([HKM20]).

For any Δ∈𝒫Σ\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}, its n+in+i-th horizontal part can be computed as

hn+i​(Δ)=(n+i)!i!​∫Δc​(λ)i​⁡d​λ​,h_{n+i}(\Delta)=\frac{(n+i)!}{i!}\int_{\Delta}c(\lambda)^{i}\mathop{}\!d\lambda\text{,}

where, as before, c:Mℝ→A1​(X)c:M_{\mathbb{R}}\to A^{1}(X) is the linear map given by c⁡(λ)=c1​(ℒλ)c(\lambda)=c_{1}({\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}) for integral λ\lambda.

Denote by PXP_{X} the potential of A∗​(X)A^{*}(X) with respect to the generating vector space A∗​(X)A^{*}(X) and by PEΣP_{E_{\Sigma}} the potential of A∗​(EΣ)A^{*}(E_{\Sigma}) with respect to A∗​(X)⊕𝒫ΣA^{*}(X)\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}. The following theorem is the main result of this section. It provides a relation between potentials PEΣP_{E_{\Sigma}} and PXP_{X}.

Theorem 5.6.

For any Δ∈𝒫Σ\Delta\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} and γ∈A∗​(X)\gamma\in A^{*}(X) we have

PEΣ​(γ,Δ)=∫ΔPX​(c⁡(λ)+γ)​⁡𝑑λ.P_{E_{\Sigma}}(\gamma,\Delta)=\int_{\Delta}P_{X}(c(\lambda)+\gamma)\mathop{}\!d\lambda.
Proof.

The proof relies on Theorem 5.5 and is a direct calculation otherwise. Recall that by Theorem 4.2, the potentials PEΣ,PXP_{E_{\Sigma}},P_{X} are given by

PEΣ=Exp∗​ℓEΣ,PX=Exp∗​ℓXP_{E_{\Sigma}}={\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}\ell_{E_{\Sigma}},\quad P_{X}={\mathrm{Exp}}^{*}\ell_{X}

In other words, the evaluations of potentials PEΣP_{E_{\Sigma}} and PXP_{X} on an elements of A∗​(X)⊕𝒫ΣA^{*}(X)\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma} and A∗​(X)A^{*}(X) respectively are given by the following formulas

PEΣ​(γ,Δ)=ℓEΣ​(∑j=0∞(p∗​(γ)+ρ⁡(Δ))jj!),PX​(γ)=ℓX​(∑j=0∞γjj!)P_{E_{\Sigma}}(\gamma,\Delta)=\ell_{E_{\Sigma}}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(p^{*}(\gamma)+\rho(\Delta))^{j}}{j!}\right),\quad P_{X}(\gamma)=\ell_{X}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\gamma^{j}}{j!}\right)

By definition of horizontal parts hi​(Δ)h_{i}(\Delta) of Δ\Delta we have

PEΣ​(γ,Δ)=ℓEΣ​(p∗​(exp⁡(γ))⋅∑j=0∞ρ​(Δ)jj!)=ℓX​(exp⁡(γ)⋅∑j=0∞hj​(Δ)j!).P_{E_{\Sigma}}(\gamma,\Delta)=\ell_{E_{\Sigma}}\left(p^{*}(\exp(\gamma))\cdot\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\rho(\Delta)^{j}}{j!}\right)=\ell_{X}\left(\exp(\gamma)\cdot\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{h_{j}(\Delta)}{j!}\right).

Now, by Theorem 5.5 we get hj​(Δ)=0h_{j}(\Delta)=0 for j<nj<n and

hn+i​(Δ)=(n+i)!i!​∫Δc​(λ)i​⁡d​λ​,h_{n+i}(\Delta)=\frac{(n+i)!}{i!}\int_{\Delta}c(\lambda)^{i}\mathop{}\!d\lambda\text{,}

otherwise. Hence we obtain

PEΣ​(γ,Δ)=ℓX​(exp⁡(γ)⋅∑j=0∞hj​(Δ)j!)=ℓX​(exp⁡(γ)⋅∑i=0∞hn+i​(Δ)(n+i)!)=ℓX​(exp⁡(γ)⋅∑i=0∞1i!​∫Δc​(λ)i​⁡dλ)=ℓX​(∫Δexp⁡(γ+c⁡(λ))​⁡dλ)=∫ΔℓX​(exp⁡(c⁡(λ)+γ))​⁡𝑑λ=∫ΔPX​(c⁡(λ)+γ)​⁡dλ,\begin{split}P_{E_{\Sigma}}(\gamma,\Delta)=\ell_{X}\left(\exp(\gamma)\cdot\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{h_{j}(\Delta)}{j!}\right)&=\ell_{X}\left(\exp(\gamma)\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{h_{n+i}(\Delta)}{(n+i)!}\right)=\\ \ell_{X}\left(\exp(\gamma)\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{i!}\int_{\Delta}c(\lambda)^{i}\mathop{}\!d\lambda\right)&=\ell_{X}\left(\int_{\Delta}\exp(\gamma+c(\lambda))\mathop{}\!d\lambda\right)=\\ \int_{\Delta}\ell_{X}(\exp(c(\lambda)+\gamma))\mathop{}\!d\lambda&=\int_{\Delta}P_{X}(c(\lambda)+\gamma)\mathop{}\!d\lambda,\end{split}

which finishes the proof. ∎

Remark 5.7.

Theorem 5.6 suggests that the function PEΣ:A∗​(X)⊕𝒫Σ→ℝP_{E_{\Sigma}}\colon A^{*}(X)\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\to{\mathbb{R}} defined by

PEΣ​(γ,Δ)=∫ΔPX​(c⁡(λ)+γ)​⁡𝑑λ.P_{E_{\Sigma}}(\gamma,\Delta)=\int_{\Delta}P_{X}(c(\lambda)+\gamma)\mathop{}\!d\lambda.

is a polynomial. Indeed, it follows from the results of [PK92a] that the integral of a polynomial over a polytope defines a polynomial function on the space of virtual polytopes.

As an immediate corollary of Theorems 5.6 and 2.3 we obtain a computation of the ring of even degree cohomologies of toric bundle. Alternative descriptions were obtained in [SU03, Hof19, HKM20].

Theorem 5.8.

Let E→XE\to X be a principle TT-bundle with dimℝM\dim_{\mathbb{R}}M even and let EΣE_{\Sigma} be a toric bundle given by a smooth projective fan Σ\Sigma. Then the ring of even degree cohomology classes A∗​(EΣ)A^{*}(E_{\Sigma}) is given by

A∗​(EΣ)=Sym⁡(A∗​(X)⊕𝒫Σ)/Ann⁡(PEΣ),A^{*}(E_{\Sigma})={\mathrm{Sym}}\big(A^{*}(X)\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\big)/{\mathrm{Ann}}(P_{E_{\Sigma}}),

where the polynomial PEΣP_{E_{\Sigma}} is given by

PEΣ​(γ,Δ)=∫ΔPX​(c⁡(λ)+γ)​⁡𝑑λ.P_{E_{\Sigma}}(\gamma,\Delta)=\int_{\Delta}P_{X}(c(\lambda)+\gamma)\mathop{}\!d\lambda.

5.4 The ring of conditions of horospherical homogeneous spaces

The ring of conditions is a version intersection theory for not-necessarily complete homogeneous space. It was introduced by De Concini and Procesi in [DCP85] as a solution to Hilbert’s 15’th problem, i.e. as a ring in which one can study classical enumerative problems. As another corollary of our main theorem, we obtain a description of the ring of conditions of horospherical homogeneous space.

Let GG be a reductive group over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} and let U⊂GU\subset G be its maximal unipotent subgroup. The subgroup H⊂GH\subset G is called horospherical if it contains UU. The homogeneous space G/HG/H is called horospherical if HH is a horospherical subgroup of GG. Let PHP_{H} be the normalizer of HH, it is well-known that PHP_{H} is a parabolic subgroup of GG, and that TH=PH/HT_{H}=P_{H}/H is an algebraic torus. Moreover, the homogeneous space G/HG/H is a total space of THT_{H}-principal bundle over generalized flag variety G/PUG/P_{U} (see for example [Pas08, Pas09] for details).

Toric bundles EΣ:=G/H×THYΣE_{\Sigma}:=G/H\times_{T_{H}}Y_{\Sigma} associated to the principle THT_{H}-bundle G/H→G/PHG/H\to G/P_{H} (also called toroidal horospherical varieties) are known to have only even degree cohomology classes. Thus Theorem 5.8 computes full cohomology rings in this case. In fact, by Bia łynicki-Birula decomposition ([BB73]), varieties EΣE_{\Sigma} have a paving by affine spaces, so that H∗​(EΣ,ℤ)H^{*}(E_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{Z}}) is torsion free. Hence, Theorem 5.8, in particular, computes integer cohomology of EΣE_{\Sigma}. Moreover, in the situation as above the ring of conditions C∗​(G/H)C^{*}(G/H) is given by

C∗​(G/H)=lim→⁡A∗​(EΣ),C^{*}(G/H)=\varinjlim A^{*}(E_{\Sigma}),

where the limit is taken over all smooth projective fans Σ\Sigma (see [DCP85, Section 6.3]).

Thus we obtain the following theorem.

Theorem 5.9.

Let G/HG/H be a horospherical homogeneous space and let EΣE_{\Sigma} be its smooth projective toroidal compactification. Then the cohomology ring H∗/2(EΣ,ℝ)=A∗(EΣ)H^{*/2}(E_{\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}})=A^{*}(E_{\Sigma}) of EΣE_{\Sigma} is given by

A∗​(EΣ)=Sym⁡(A∗​(G/PH)⊕𝒫Σ)/Ann⁡(PG/H),A^{*}(E_{\Sigma})={\mathrm{Sym}}\big(A^{*}(G/P_{H})\oplus{\mathcal{P}}_{\Sigma}\big)/{\mathrm{Ann}}(P_{G/H}),

where A∗​(G/PH)A^{*}(G/P_{H}) is the cohomology ring of G/PHG/P_{H} and

PG/H​(γ,Δ)=∫ΔPG/PH​(c⁡(λ)+γ)​⁡𝑑λ.P_{G/H}(\gamma,\Delta)=\int_{\Delta}P_{G/P_{H}}(c(\lambda)+\gamma)\mathop{}\!d\lambda.

Moreover the ring of conditions of G/HG/H is given by

C∗​(G/H)=Sym⁡(A∗​(G/PH)⊕𝒫)/Ann⁡(PG/H).C^{*}(G/H)={\mathrm{Sym}}\big(A^{*}(G/P_{H})\oplus{\mathcal{P}}\big)/{\mathrm{Ann}}(P_{G/H}).
